query: For high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what testable methodological hypothesis could enable improved combinations of strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance? Explain why it should work, what measurable improvement is expected relative to the state of the art, the conditions under which it should or should not hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experimental result that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A short‐to‐medium time annealing treatment applied after hot‐rolling a CrCoNi‐based high‐entropy alloy induces an optimal level of atomic short‐range order (SRO) that simultaneously enhances strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance relative to the standard as‐rolled/quenched state.
generation.material_initial_state: A hot‐rolled CrCoNi-based high-entropy (or medium-entropy) alloy with an FCC single-phase structure exhibiting a conventional balance of strength (~350 MPa yield), ductility, and modulus but limited fracture resistance.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled annealing process (performed in an inert atmosphere at a temperature chosen to initiate SRO without significant grain growth) immediately following hot rolling.
generation.conditions: Annealing to be executed under nonoxidizing conditions at a temperature below the full recrystallization point (with temperature and time chosen based on preliminary studies to trigger SRO formation) and subsequent testing under room-temperature structural loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced atomic short-range order (SRO) at the nanoscale, which may also promote beneficial nanoscale twins/precipitates that stabilize the FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The annealing treatment promotes atomic reordering that increases local bond strength and creates a fine-scale structural heterogeneity. This SRO impedes dislocation motion (increasing strength and modulus) while also facilitating intrinsic toughening (improving ductility and fracture resistance) by enabling mechanisms such as dislocation accumulation and crack-tip shielding.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-hot rolled/quenched control, the annealed alloy should exhibit a measurable improvement in yield strength, higher Young’s modulus, enhanced fracture resistance, and retained or improved ductility. The magnitude of improvement is expected to be significant relative to the current state-of-the-art, although precise values are not predetermined.
generation.baseline: CrCoNi-based high-entropy alloy processed by hot rolling and rapid quenching, lacking the targeted SRO-inducing annealing step.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to hold only when the annealing temperature-time parameters are optimized. Excessively high temperatures or too long annealing durations that cause grain coarsening, oxidation, or unwanted phase transformations would likely negate the beneficial SRO effects.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative gains in mechanical properties depend sensitively on the annealing parameters and may vary with subtle differences in alloy composition; further experimental optimization is needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrCoNi-based HEA samples: (a) a control set processed by hot rolling followed by rapid quenching, and (b) an experimental set that, after hot rolling, undergoes a short-to-medium annealing treatment at a temperature chosen to promote SRO. Characterize both sets using atom probe tomography (APT) to quantify SRO and perform standard tensile, dynamic mechanical analysis, and fracture toughness tests at room temperature.
measurements: Quantification of short-range order via APT
Tensile tests to determine yield strength and ductility
Dynamic mechanical analysis to measure Young’s modulus
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a significant increase in SRO relative to the control, or if they fail to exhibit improved yield strength, ductility, modulus, or fracture toughness (or if these properties worsen), then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Medium- and high-entropy alloys are an emerging class of materials that can exhibit outstanding combinations of strength and ductility for engineering applications. Computational simulations have suggested the presence of short-range order (SRO) in these alloys, and recent experimental evidence is also beginning to emerge. Unfortunately, the difficulty in quantifying the SRO under different heat treatment conditions has generated much debate on the atomic preferencing and implications of SRO on mechanical properties. Here we develop an approach to measure SRO using atom probe tomography. This method balances the limitations of atom probe tomography with the threshold values of SRO to map the regimes where the required atomistic neighbourhood information is preserved and where it is not. We demonstrate the method with a case study of the CoCrNi alloy and use this to monitor SRO changes induced by heat treatments. These species-specific SRO measurements enable the generation of computational simulations of atomic neighbourhood models that are equivalent to the experiment and can contribute to the further understanding and design of medium- and high-entropy alloys and other materials

As a class of advanced metal materials, high/medium-entropy alloys (H/MEAs) hold great promise for overcoming the property bottleneck in conventional alloys [,]. Among many studies [,,], an equiatomic CrCoNi MEA with a face-centered cubic (FCC) structure has emerged as one of the most damage-tolerant alloys to date. Despite its excellent ductility, the alloy always showed a lower yield strength of approximately 350 MPa, because of the multiple slip systems, similar to other FCC alloys []. This severely limits its engineering serviceability for structural applications. Exploring appropriate strategies to overcome the strength–ductility trade-off has been a major objective for the CrCoNi MEA [].
